newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky arrives in Albania to push elections.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky arrives in Albania to push elections.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky arrived in troubled Albania on Wednesday to discuss elections due on June 29 as Italy threatened to withdraw its troops if the vote was put off.

Former Austrian Chancellor Vranitzky, envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), made no comment as he arrived in Tirana on his third trip since widespread rioting over failed pyramid savings schemes pushed the Balkan country to the brink of anarchy in March.
Vranitzky was due to meet interim Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino later in the day. He was also to see President Sali Berisha.

The European envoy was expected to try to resolve the deadlock between Fino and Berisha that threatens to scupper the elections agreed when a government of National Reconciliation was set up in March.
Fino has threatened to resign unless the Albanian parliament, dominated by Berisha's Democratic Party, passes a new law increasing the number of seats to be elected by proportional representation.
Fino's Socialist Party and the Democratic Party have failed in five meetings to agree on the election law.
He has said the nine-party interim government will now pass the new law by majority and send it for approval by parliament.

Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta told the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) in Rome on Wednesday that the multinational force in Albania to secure humanitarian aid supplies should be withdrawn if the agreement to hold elections by the end of June is broken.

Italy heads the eight-nation 6,000-strong force. Although its U.N. mandate limits the force to securing aid deliveries, its very presence has helped to calm Albania after a wave of violence in which several hundred people were killed.
Many Albanians are hoping the mandate of the force will be extended to allow it to provide security for the election and ensure it is free and fair.

The Socialists withdrew from last May's elections late on polling day, complaining of fraud. International monitors agreed that the vote, which gave Berisha's party 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament, was seriously flawed. The election deadlock must be resolved over the next few days if the vote is to be held on schedule.
Albanian law requires the president to issue a decree calling the election at least 45 days before it is held, meaning he has another eight days if the vote is to take place by June 29.

Berisha is demanding the abolition of salvation committees -- citizens' groups that sprang up in southern Albania as the state disintegrated. He says they are armed political forces and make a free and fair election impossible.
Fino denies his Socialists are linked to the committees and has said they should disband after an election date is set.
Residents of the south say many of the committees have already broken up.
